response.answer: For exposure-aware ranking, use metrics like demographic parity and equalized odds to ensure fair representation of small tourism subgroups. Evaluate with offline testing to measure group-specific recommendation quality. Focus on minimizing popularity bias to protect underrepresented items.

results.title: A survey on popularity bias in recommender systems - Springer Nature
results.content: In terms of underlying research motivations, most examined works are based on the application-*independent* assumption that focusing on popular items is problematic *per se* and causes potential consequences such as limited exposure of certain items, the reinforcement of biases, and limited recommendation quality for users by default. In certain cases, the authors consider solely accuracy metrics for the evaluation, but measuring it separately for groups of users and items to demonstrate that recommendation quality for niche users or items can be affected by popularity bias. Clearly, offline experimentation will remain to have its place in research, e.g., to investigate if one algorithm has a stronger tendency to recommend popular items than another one or if popularity bias may lead to reinforcement effects in a longitudinal perspective, see, e.g., Jannach et al. Recommender systems that have a bias towards recommending mostly popular items may be of limited value both for users and for providers, and such systems may even exert harmful effects in certain application settings. *et al.* A survey on popularity bias in recommender systems.
